_note: Plain-English glosses for the abbreviation signs that actually occur in the exercise bank. `status` is load-bearing: `verified` = the expansion comes from a source AND the source page was read as an image (the chocomufin table shipped with the Eutyches dataset; Thompson 1912; Cappelli 1929 -- see research/cappelli-index.md for the leaf of every sign); `proposed` = standard palaeographic convention, mine, AWAITING WILSON'S RATIFICATION. Never silently promote one to the other. `mechanism` follows Thompson 1912 ch. VII: a CONTRACTION keeps the word's ending so the inflection survives; a SUSPENSION cuts the end off and destroys it.

signs.name: the abbreviation stroke
signs.short: a stroke over a letter: something has been left out
signs.note: The commonest mark in Latin manuscripts, and the least specific — it says only that letters are missing. Over a vowel it is an omitted m or n (Cappelli, Lexicon Abbreviaturarum (1929), p. XXIV: cōdo=conditio, ī=in). Over a c it is cum, con, cen (p. XXX) — in this book c̃sidero is considero. At a word's end it can be -er: frequent̃ is frequenter. Cappelli devotes a whole section to signs like this — segni abbreviativi con significato relativo, p. XXIX — signs whose value is not fixed but changes with the letter they are attached to. That is why an abbreviation table can never be a simple list of one sign, one meaning.

signs.name: u with a stroke
signs.note: A vowel carrying the stroke has lost a following m or n. locũ is locum. This is the single most frequent abbreviation in the whole corpus — worth knowing cold before anything else.

signs.name: a with a stroke
signs.note: The same stroke on an a: an omitted m or n follows.

signs.name: o with a stroke
signs.note: The same stroke on an o. cõmouere is commouere — note the doubled m is not written twice.

signs.name: i with a stroke
signs.note: The same stroke on an i. Very often the whole word in.

signs.name: p with a stroke through the descender
signs.note: The stroke crosses the descender of the p. Cappelli, Lexicon Abbreviaturarum (1929), p. XXX, gives it as per, par… por… — read confirmed on the plate. Its near neighbour ꝓ, with a loop rather than a bar, is pro (Cappelli p. XXXVIII); learn the two as a pair so you never confuse them.

signs.name: q with a stroke through the descender
signs.short: ꝗ = qui — but see the date
signs.note: Cappelli p. XXX gives q̶ = qui. ⚠ His footnote matters for us: “Nel sec. VIII lo stesso segno vale que” — in the eighth century the same sign means que, and in Anglo-Saxon writing quam or quia. Our manuscripts are ninth-century, sitting right on that boundary, so read the sentence before you trust the sign.

signs.name: a written above the line
signs.short: a small a above a letter supplies that vowel — qͣ = qua
signs.note: A vowel written small and high belongs immediately after the letter it sits on. Over a q it gives qua: aliqͣ is aliqua, and qͣsi is quasi. The same trick with a small i gives qui, with a small o, quo. Once you see it as a letter that has simply climbed above the line, it stops being strange.

signs.name: the us-sign
signs.note: A word-ending sign, standing on the line after the last written letter: c̃seruatꝰ is conservatus. Verified against the character table shipped with this dataset.

signs.name: the ur-sign
signs.note: A small hook above the line at a word's end: seruat᷑ is seruatur. This one matters for reading sense, because -ur is what makes a Latin verb passive. Verified against this dataset's character table.

signs.name: the est-sign
signs.note: A whole word in one mark. Its dataset character table names it outright, and Thompson gives the same. When a sentence seems to have no verb, look for this.

signs.name: the Tironian et
signs.note: Not a letter at all: a surviving sign from the ancient Roman shorthand attributed to Cicero's secretary Tiro. It outlived the rest of that system by a thousand years, and is still written in Irish today.

signs.name: l with a stroke
signs.short: ł = vel (and, inside a word, ul or el)
signs.note: Cappelli p. XXX: ł = vel, ul…, …el. So it is not always the word ‘or’: crossing the ascender of an l mid-word it can simply supply ul or el. In a grammar book, which spends its life saying a form may be this or that, vel is still much the likeliest.

signs.name: d with a stroke
signs.short: đ = a d-word, most often quod as qđ
signs.note: Rarely alone. You will nearly always meet it as qđ = quod.

signs.name: e caudata, the e with a tail
signs.note: Not an abbreviation at all but a spelling: the little tail is how the Middle Ages wrote the diphthong ae. ecclesię is ecclesiae. If you read it as a plain e, the case ending will mislead you.

signs.name: round brackets — the editors' supply
signs.short: ( ) = letters supplied because the ink cannot be read
signs.note: These letters are not on the page. Where the ink is lost the editors restored what the word must have been and put it in brackets. Verified by reading the manuscript itself at four places: purple mould stains sitting over the words; ink simply worn away; a gloss too faint to make out; and, in one case, a tear that has taken the parchment clean away. Do not hunt for them in the ink — there is nothing there. Damage of this kind is ordinary; a thousand-year-old book has been rained on, handled, and eaten by mould, and part of reading manuscripts is knowing what your edition is quietly doing for you.

signs.name: the enlarged opening initial
signs.short: a big letter out in the margin — it is the word's first letter
signs.note: A new section opens with a large decorated capital set out in the margin, clear of the ruled text block and often two lines deep. The scribe does not write the letter twice. So the ordinary script begins with the SECOND letter: the line here starts uaeritur, the tall Q beside it supplies the first, and together they are Quaeritur. Verified on the page (Cod. 940 f. 30). Once you know to look for it this is a help rather than a trap — it tells you a new argument is beginning.

signs.name: the et-ligature
signs.short: & is e and t written as one — and it works INSIDE a word
signs.note: Our ampersand began life as a ligature of e and t, and in a manuscript it has not yet settled into meaning only the word et. The scribe uses it for the letters e-t wherever they fall, including in the middle or at the end of a word: this line's ink reads ſupl& and the word is suplet. Likewise hab& for habet, man& for manet. ⚠ Do not confuse it with the Tironian ⁊, which is a shorthand sign for the word et and never supplies a syllable. Verified on the page (Cod. 940 f. 41).

signs.name: word division
signs.short: the gaps between words are not where you expect them
signs.note: Ancient books were written in scriptio continua — no spaces at all. Word division was introduced gradually, and in the ninth century the job is only half done. Short words cling to their neighbours, and a gap can open in the middle of a long one. On this page the ink reads quarequomodolongitudinem where the print gives Quare quomodo longitudinem. ⚑ So do not trust the gaps. Read a run of letters, find a word you know inside it, and let the rest fall out — the Latin divides the line, not the spacing. This is the single thing that most often defeats a reader who can already name every letter.
